Introduction¶

The COVID-19 quarantine lasted over a year and affected all aspects of life worldwide. The Household Pulse Survey, which is a series of surveys by the U.S. Census Bureau, was designed to gauge the impact of the pandemic. The survey entails employment status, consumer spending, food security, housing, education disruptions, and dimensions of physical and mental wellness. A subset of this data that focuses on mental health was published for public use by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on its official website. It was also published by the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services in the U.S. government's open data source, Data.gov. Data.gov was launched in 2009 and is managed and hosted by the U.S. General Services Administration, Technology Transformation Services. It is a reliable source because it is managed by government entities, which means its data-keeping procedures are excellent. The subset was extracted from Data.gov as a CSV file titled Indicators of Anxiety or Depression Based on Reported Frequency of Symptoms During Last 7 Days. Although the survey was conducted post time period, it begins to account for data from April 4th, 2020, to September 16, 2024.

Methodology¶

According to the Data.gov website, the survey was "conducted by an internet questionnaire, with invitations to participate sent by email and text message". To rapidly monitor the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on U.S. Households. The portion of the survey that measures mental illness symptoms was a collaborative effort between the National Center for Health Statistics(NCHS) partnered with the U.S. Census Bureau. The complete Household Pulse Survey (HPS) survey was experimental, online, and (approximately) 20 minutes long. Housing units linked to one or more email addresses or cell phone numbers were randomly selected to participate, and one respondent per unit was selected to respond on his or her own behalf. This introduces coverage limitations, since individuals without reliable internet access or updated contact information may be underrepresented. 19% of households without email/phone excluded from the sampling frame (U.S. Census Bureau). If email or phone records were not linked to a respondent’s current residence, the geographic identifiers assigned in the dataset may be inaccurate. Due to these potential issues with geographic validity and representativeness, state-level or regional analyses were not included in this project.This also means the data is from randomly sampled individuals in households, not single-person households. Many variables can differ between the living situations of multiple people and those of individuals. Among these variables is where one stands within the household dynamics. The pandemic may impact homeowners differently than tenants, vice versa, or similarly. There are vast variables that cannot be accounted for when analyzing the data.

The "Time Period" is a distinguishing variable when considering the impacts the COVID-19 pandemic had on individuals in households. It specifies the range of the dates during which survey responses were collected for each observation. Each time period spans approximately 7 to 13 days, reflecting one wave of data collection within the U.S. Household Pulse Survey. They occur sequentially with minimal gaps and correspond to distinct survey waves within larger survey phases. There were several methodological considerations taken into account when analyzing this data. The "Time Period" variable is an ordered, discrete measure of time rather than a continuous variable. Thus data was sorted chronologically to ensure accurate trend visualization. Since each period covers approximately a week, the data captures weekly fluctuations and longer-term trends without excessive interpretation. Often, the phase divisions coincided with changes in question wording, sample size, or demographics. For this reason, analysis was conducted both within and across phases. This allows for direct comparisons between phases that may reflect design changes or true population shifts. Not every phase includes all demographics, subgroups, or indicators. Other variables were introduced in the later phases, leading to inconsistent data due to changes in structure. This was accounted for by excluding those variables when making comparisons: disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, health insurance status, and vaccination status. The findings over time may be influenced by a combination of societal shifts and survey modifications. The “By Gender Identity” group was also excluded from the analysis. This decision aligns with the data-cleaning approach described earlier, where subgroup categories that were not directly comparable to demographic variables were removed. Gender identity categories contain small sample sizes and produce highly variable or unstable estimates, which distorts the interpretation of broader population trends. To maintain consistency and focus the analysis, all rows associated with “By Gender identity” were excluded from the dataset. Screening for mental indicators was based on adapted PHQ-2 (depression) and GAD-2 (anxiety) screening questions. Response options: not at all (0), several days (1), more than half the days (2), and nearly every day (3). A score ≥3 on the PHQ-2 is associated with major depressive disorder, and a score ≥3 on the GAD-2 is associated with generalized anxiety disorder. The HPS indicators used in this project represent the percentage of adults with scores at or above this clinical threshold.

The original CSV file for the Indicators of Anxiety or Depression Based on Reported Frequency of Symptoms During the Last 7 Days contains fourteen variables. Several columns represent demographic classifications, including Group, State, and Subgroup. The dataset also includes multiple time-related variables: Phase, Time Period, Time Period Label, Time Period Start Date, and Time Period End Date. They describe the survey wave in which each observation was collected. Most variables contain the full 16,794 entries. However, four estimation-related columns—Value, Low CI, High CI, and Confidence Interval—are missing exclusively for observations that represent non-state groups. In other words, rows associated with national-level categories(such as “United States,” “By Age,” or “By Race/Ethnicity”) are far more likely to lack published estimates and confidence intervals. This indicates that the missingness is not random but instead reflects structural features of the survey design. The Household Pulse Survey prioritizes state-level estimates and does not always compute or release estimates for every demographic subgroup at the national level. When sample sizes are insufficient or a subgroup is not included in the model for a particular phase, the survey omits the estimate entirely. These omissions lead to gaps in the four estimation columns for non-state groups, while state-specific rows remain largely complete.

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
sns.barplot(
    data=df_1,
    x="Group",           
    y="Value",           
    hue="Indicator",     # diff colors for indicators
    errorbar = 'sd',             # shows the standard deviation as error bars

)

plt.ylabel("Estimated Percentage (%)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right")

Each bar represents the mean percentage of adults reporting symptoms within each demographic group. The colors represent different mental health indicators as shown in the top left legend.

Analysis of Anxiety by Subgroups¶

In [24]:
excluded_subgroups = [
    "With disability", "Without disability",
    "Gay or lesbian", "Bisexual", "Straight", "Something else",
    "Transgender", "Not transgender",
    "Has health insurance", "Does not have health insurance",
    "Vaccinated", "Not vaccinated"

Several subgroup categories were excluded to avoid inappropriate comparisons. Specifically, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, health insurance status, and vaccination status were removed because these categories are not directly comparable to socioeconomic, race, or age-based subgroups.

In [25]:
df_2 = df_1[~df_1["Subgroup"].isin(excluded_subgroups)]
In [26]:
anxiety_df = df_2[df_2["Indicator"] == "Symptoms of Anxiety Disorder"]
In [27]:
age_anxiety = anxiety_df[anxiety_df["Group"] == "By Age"]

plt.figure(figsize=(12,6))
sns.boxplot(data= age_anxiety, x="Subgroup", y="Value",color= "#FF0074")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.title("Anxiety Levels by Adult Age Group")
plt.ylabel("Reported Anxiety (%)")
plt.xlabel("Age Group")

plt.show()

Anxiety levels decrease consistently with age. Young adults (18–29) show the highest anxiety percentages, while older adults 60 and above report much lower and more stable levels. This pattern indicates that younger adults experienced the anxiety-inducing distress during the pandemic, with anxiety steadily declining across older age groups.

In [28]:

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
ax = sns.barplot(
    data=age_means,

ax.bar_label(

    fmt="%.1f",

This bar chart aligns with the pattern shown in the previous boxplot: average anxiety levels decrease with age. The mean anxiety percentages align with the medians and distributions from the earlier graph. Anxiety was highest among adults 18–29 and progressively lower in older age groups. The chart summarizes this trend.

In [22]:
race_df = anxiety_df[anxiety_df["Group"] == "By Race/Hispanic ethnicity"]

plt.figure(figsize=(12,6))
sns.boxplot(data=race_df, x="Subgroup", y="Value",color= "#FF0074")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.title("Anxiety Levels by Race/Ethnicity")
plt.ylabel("Reported Anxiety (%)")
plt.xlabel("Race/Ethnicity")
plt.show()

The boxplots above show the anxiety levels across racial and ethnic groups. Hispanic or Latino adults and Non-Hispanic adults of "other races and multiple races" show the highest anxiety levels, with higher medians and wider spreads. Non-Hispanic Asian adults report the lowest anxiety levels overall, with a much lower median and wider distribution. Non-Hispanic White and Non-Hispanic Black adults fall in between, with Non-Hispanic White having a smaller spread and a lower median. Overall, the graph shows meaningful racial and ethnic differences, with some groups experiencing substantially higher anxiety than others.

In [43]:
edu_df = anxiety_df[anxiety_df["Group"] == "By Education"]

plt.figure(figsize=(12,6))
sns.boxplot(data = edu_df, x="Subgroup", y="Value",color= "#FF0074")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.title("Anxiety Levels by Education Level")
plt.ylabel("Reported Anxiety (%)")
plt.xlabel("Education Level")
plt.show()

Anxiety levels tend to decrease as education increases. Adults with less than a high school diploma report the highest anxiety levels, with the largest spread and the highest median. Anxiety is moderately lower among those with a high school diploma or some college, but the decline becomes most noticeable among adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher—the group with the lowest and tightest distribution of anxiety scores. Overall, higher educational attainment is associated with lower reported anxiety.

Because the missingness is systematic and reflects measurement limitations rather than random data loss, no imputation was performed. Analysis involving these estimation variables was restricted to observations with the available values.

In [17]:
df_1 = pd.read_csv('Indicators_of_Anxiety_or_Depression_Based_on_Reported_Frequency_of_Symptoms_During_Last_7_Days.csv')

Making a copy of the dataframe was attempted, which appeared successful. Problems arose when trying to edit columns because the copy was actually a series. The CSV file was read twice. The second dataframe created from the original CSV file is meant to be edited; meanwhile, the first is kept intact for referencing.

In [18]:
df_1.columns = df_1.columns.astype(str)
In [19]:
print(df_1.columns.tolist())

['Indicator', 'Group', 'State', 'Subgroup', 'Phase', 'Time Period', 'Time Period Label', 'Time Period Start Date', 'Time Period End Date', 'Value', 'Low CI', 'High CI', 'Confidence Interval', 'Quartile Range']
In [20]:
df_1.columns = df_1.columns.str.strip()

The data cleaning process begins with the removal of any leading and trailing whitespace characters, including spaces, tabs, and newlines. This assures that changes to the columns can be made because column names are recognized with no minor errors in spelling.

In [21]:
df_1["Time Period Start Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df_1["Time Period Start Date"], errors = 'coerce')
df_1["Time Period End Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df_1["Time Period End Date"], errors = 'coerce')

The character entries in "Time Period Start Date" and "Time Period End Date" are converted to datetime objects. This allows for easier time series observations.

In [22]:
df_1 = df_1.drop(columns=["Time Period Label"], errors="ignore")

The Time Period Label column was removed because it was redundant. The start and end dates for each period are already provided in separate date columns, and the Time Period variable numerically identifies each period. Since the label does not add new information on what these variables contain, it was dropped to streamline the dataset.

Conclusions¶

This analysis shows that symptoms of anxiety and depression differed significantly throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Anxiety levels were consistently higher than depression levels, and the combined “anxiety or depression” indicator remained the highest across all time periods. This shows the psychological strain experienced by the U.S. adult population during the COVID-19 pandemic. Time-series patterns indicate that symptom levels peaked early in the pandemic and gradually declined over later survey periods, suggesting that emotional distress eased as social and economic conditions stabilized. Demographic comparisons revealed clear disparities in age groups: younger adults (18–29) consistently reported the highest levels of anxiety and depression, while older adults (65+) reported the lowest levels across all three indicators. Women also showed higher symptom rates than men throughout the dataset. Racial and ethnic patterns showed additional variability, with Hispanic or Latino adults and Non-Hispanic adults of “other races and multiple races” exhibiting elevated anxiety levels, while Non-Hispanic Asian adults reported the lowest levels. Together, these results indicate that while population-level psychological distress eased over time, the mental burden remained unevenly distributed.

There are limitations such as nonresponse bias and coverage issues. In other words, those who did not respond to mental health questions were excluded from the data set completely. Additionally, all respondents had access to either an email or a phone number, which was used to identify them to a geographical area. This limits the sampling to individuals with familiarity with technology and internet access. If emails or phone numbers were not updated geographically, then state information could be inaccurate. For this reason, the geographical analysis was not explored in this report.
